title: Intelligence Isn't All It's Cracked Up to Be
subtitle: The Age of AI is Trying to Teach Everyone a Lesson I Learned Hard

blocks.html: Growing up, almost everything that other people found difficult and impressive came easily to me. This delighted my parents, themselves middle-class strivers who clawed their way into medical school after worthless humanities degrees. Life working out for them was down to good test scores and following instructions. They felt reassured and validated as parents when I would bring home a piece of paper with a red "100" at the top.

I loved tests; they were opportunities to show how much better I was than other people. It goes without saying that my classmates did not like me. But when word got back to my mom and dad, they urged me to be patient. If the other kids were not friendly, my parents told me, it was because they envied my ability. Someday I would be among peers and those peers would appreciate me for my ability to contribute, my willingness to work hard, my integrity, and my pleasant manner and presentation. Needless to say, it was lonely. Even after I had grown up, met the world, been crushed and humbled by how wrong I had it all—getting high scores would still reassure me that I had something to offer.

But I think the thrill is gone. Mere intelligence is all but bottled. Some highly credentialed humans reveal by their behavior that they already believe AI is smart enough to do their jobs—otherwise lawyers and judges would not be filing AI-authored briefs and opinions, public figures issuing AI-written statements, academic administrators submitting AI-generated articles for publication in journals. Although I do not believe any AI model can fashion a fresh and enduring stage- or screenplay yet, I don't deny that may not be far off.

It's difficult for most people to grasp how rare extremely high intelligence is. An IQ of 135 places an individual in the 99th percentile, meaning that a group of 100 people contains an average of one individual who tests at that level. The distribution of intelligence is such that the likelihood a random group of 100 contains someone of IQ 135+ is about 63%. A group of 69 people already gives a 50% chance.

145 is quite different. To have a 50% chance of encountering a person with IQ 145+, you need a random sample of 502 people. In a random sample of 1,000 people, there remains a 25% chance you will not encounter anyone at this level.

It is only through the sacred love of Jesus that I understand why the value of my own intelligence and talent are not threatened (and are really enhanced) by these developments that promise to commodify and cheapen hard-won skills that I once meant to bind into my sense of who I am.
